sections.title: Statement and Assumption at an Advanced Level
sections.content: At Level 3, the task is to identify the subtle philosophical, logical, and nuanced ideas hidden behind the statement. The assumption is often not obvious but remains concealed as the foundation of the reasoning. In exams, options are often worded very similarly, so identifying the correct assumption requires careful attention to the words and scope of the statement.

sections.title: Philosophical Assumptions
sections.content: Some statements are based on ethical or philosophical principles. For example, utilitarian thinking assumes that the correct decision is the one that benefits the greatest number of people. In contrast, deontological thinking assumes that certain duties or principles must always be followed regardless of the outcome. In such questions, identifying the ethical foundation behind the statement is important.

sections.title: Paradoxical Statements
sections.content: Sometimes a statement appears contradictory at first glance. However, there is usually a hidden logic that connects the two ideas. Recognizing this hidden logical bridge is the correct assumption. Without that bridge, the statement would appear inconsistent or illogical.

sections.title: Nuance and Extreme Words Trap
sections.content: At Level 3, many options contain extreme words such as 'all', 'never', 'always', or 'none'. These strong words often make the assumption incorrect because the statement itself does not claim something so absolute. In contrast, options with softer and limited language are usually more logically consistent.

sections.title: Understanding the Scope of the Argument
sections.content: Understanding the scope of the statement is very important. If the statement refers to a specific situation or group, the assumption must remain within that same boundary. If an option expands the scope to the entire society or all situations, it is often incorrect.

sections.title: 4–6 Step Logical Evaluation Method
sections.content: Step 1: Read the statement carefully and understand its main objective. Step 2: Identify the principle, policy, or reasoning on which the statement is based. Step 3: Determine which idea has been assumed to be true without being explicitly stated. Step 4: Examine the scope and intensity of the words used in the option. Step 5: Negate the option and check whether the statement becomes weak. Step 6: Ensure that the option forms the foundation of the statement rather than a future result or general knowledge.

sections.title: Outside Knowledge Trap
sections.content: Assumptions should be evaluated only based on the given statement. Introducing external knowledge or personal experiences may lead to incorrect conclusions. In examinations, the correct answer will always be the one that is logically necessary based on the statement alone.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Accepting overly broad options as correct. 2. Including personal experiences in the reasoning process. 3. Treating future consequences as assumptions. 4. Ignoring the limits of the words used in the statement.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 3, identifying assumptions requires deep logical understanding. It is important to recognize philosophical foundations, paradoxical reasoning, and subtle language differences. The correct assumption is the one that supports the fundamental logic hidden behind the statement.

tricks.title: Core Principle Identification Trick
tricks.explanation: Sometimes a statement is based on an ethical or principle-based belief. Identifying that core principle helps locate the correct assumption.
tricks.example: Statement: The government restricted private vehicles to reduce pollution. Assumption: Collective welfare is more important than individual convenience.

tricks.title: Paradox Bridge Trick
tricks.explanation: If a statement appears contradictory, find the hidden idea that connects the two parts.
tricks.example: Statement: Sometimes working less can increase productivity. Assumption: Excessive work may cause fatigue and reduce efficiency.

tricks.title: Extreme Word Trap
tricks.explanation: Be cautious when options contain words like 'always', 'never', or 'all'. Statements rarely support such absolute claims.
tricks.example: Statement: Some people prefer online education. Option: All people prefer online education. This is an incorrect assumption.

tricks.title: Scope Check Trick
tricks.explanation: Identify the scope of the statement and choose an assumption within that same boundary.
tricks.example: Statement: Some schools in the city installed digital boards. Assumption: Students in those schools may benefit from digital learning.

tricks.title: Necessary Link Test
tricks.explanation: An assumption is the logical link that connects the reasoning. Without it, the argument collapses.
tricks.example: Statement: The company started training programs to improve performance. Assumption: Training can enhance employees' abilities.

tricks.title: Negation Technique
tricks.explanation: Reverse the assumption and see whether the statement becomes weak.
tricks.example: If training does not improve ability at all, the purpose of the program becomes weak.

tricks.title: Inference Trap Identification
tricks.explanation: If an option is a conclusion derived from the statement, it is an inference, not an assumption.
tricks.example: Statement: The company launched a new product. Option: The company will become the market leader. This is a result, not an assumption.

tricks.title: Hidden Value System
tricks.explanation: Many statements are based on an underlying value system or priority.
tricks.example: Statement: The university prioritized research activities. Assumption: Research improves academic quality.

tricks.title: Language Precision Rule
tricks.explanation: At Level 3, the correct answer often depends on subtle wording differences, so read carefully.
tricks.example: Statement: Some employees supported the new policy. Assumption: At least some employees consider the policy useful.

tricks.title: Logical Bridge Identification
tricks.explanation: The hidden logical connection between the action and its objective is the assumption.
tricks.example: Statement: The city increased the number of parks to improve public health. Assumption: Parks encourage people to engage in physical activity.
